input_packet.case_brief: PhD student must choose a dissertation direction while advisor retirement, cross-lab politics, and possible visa/funding constraints make the sequence sensitive.
input_packet.anchor_visible_candidate: Option 3 sounds like the best direction if you can get the data. It keeps your existing tumor-evolution strength while connecting you to the single-cell field. Talk to the single-cell postdoc, test whether the collaboration is real, and fall back to the standard lab project if the data path fails.
input_packet.deck_pressure_candidate: Option 3 is the best candidate, but the order matters. First ask your advisor whether he supports the cross-lab direction, whether funding covers it, and whether he would accept a real co-advisor. Only then approach the single-cell postdoc with a specific methods proposal and ask what data access, authorship, and PI approval would require. Do not commit with the committee until data access and funding are real. Pre-commit now to an 18-month checkpoint: if there is no publishable result on the pipeline by then, pivot to a narrower tumor-evolution project while you still have time.

step6_output.answer_core:
Option 3 is the strongest direction: it builds on your existing tumor-evolution expertise while opening a concrete bridge to single-cell methods. Because the context is sensitive—advisor retirement, cross-lab politics, and visa/funding constraints—sequence matters.

First, meet with your advisor to confirm he supports the cross-lab direction, whether funding covers it, and whether he would accept a real co-advisor arrangement. Do not proceed to the next step until you have clear, documented answers on these three points.

Second, only then approach the single-cell postdoc with a specific methods proposal. Ask directly what data access would require, what authorship expectations are, and what PI approval is needed. Treat this as a feasibility audit, not a commitment.

Third, do not formalize anything with your committee until data access and funding are real and documented.

Set a hard 18-month checkpoint: if you do not have a publishable pipeline result by then, pivot to a narrower, self-contained tumor-evolution project within your home lab while you still have time to graduate. That fallback protects you if the cross-lab bridge collapses, but the sequencing above gives it the best chance of surviving.
